metadata.title: The Birthday Paradox: Three Things You Could Change
metadata.note: audio is the clock; reveal_cues are on the Whisper word clock (mp3/timings.json); not hand-edited

beats.title: THE BET
beats.narration_text: Twenty three people in a room. Bet me two of them share a birthday. Most people take the other side. They lose that bet about half the time, and I want to show you exactly how I know.
beats.on_screen: empty calendar grid, 23 dots drop in, two land in one cell; the counter ends the beat at 50.7%.

beats.title: THE PLAN
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI. Three things could change that odds figure: how many people are in the group, how uneven the birthdays are, and how many days they have to land on. I'll change each one and watch the number. One of them barely matters, one matters the way you'd expect, and one decides almost everything. Hold a guess about which.
beats.on_screen: three labelled cards appear and stay on screen as the chapter index: PEOPLE, EVENNESS, DAYS. The counter sits beneath them.

beats.title: WHY TWENTY THREE
beats.narration_text: The trick is to stop counting people and count pairs. Twenty three people make two hundred and fifty three pairs. Each pair is a small chance, and two hundred and fifty three small chances pile up faster than your gut expects.
beats.on_screen: lines connect the dots; the pair counter spins to 253. Do not animate this as a sum.

beats.title: PEOPLE
beats.narration_text: First change: the people. I run four hundred thousand random groups of twenty three and count how often a pair shares a day. Fifty point seven percent. The exact calculation agrees. Now add people. With ten, about twelve percent. With thirty, seventy one percent. With fifty, ninety seven percent. By fifty seven people, past ninety nine percent. More people, more odds, just as you'd expect.
beats.on_screen: the counter fills to 50.7% beside "exact 50.73%"; then dots are added one at a time with 10, 30, 50, 57 flagged and printed with percentages (held ≥2 s).
beats.source_line: "Our simulation: 400,000 groups, seed 2701. Exact calculation also shown."

beats.title: MATCH ME
beats.narration_text: One thing the claim does not say. It says some pair, not a pair with you. For somebody to share your birthday, you need two hundred and fifty three other people to reach even odds. With twenty two others in the room, your chance is under six percent. Same crowd, a different question.
beats.on_screen: "any pair" vs "someone with you" printed side by side: 23 people / 253 others; 50.7% / 5.9%, held ≥2 s.

beats.title: THE FALSE ASSUMPTION
beats.narration_text: Second change: how even the days are. So far every day was equally likely, and that's false. I used federal counts of babies born each day. They come from the National Center for Health Statistics and the Social Security Administration, and cover two thousand to two thousand fourteen. The busiest day runs about twelve percent above average. February twenty ninth runs at about a quarter of a normal day, because it only exists one year in four.
beats.on_screen: the grid recolours by real daily share with a scale; Feb 29 nearly dark with the label "exists one year in four". The credit line stays on screen for the whole beat.
beats.source_line: "Births data: US NCHS and SSA via FiveThirtyEight (CC BY 4.0)."

beats.title: THE REAL CALENDAR
beats.narration_text: So I ran it again on the real calendar. Fifty point eight percent, against fifty point seven for even days. Uneven days can only raise the odds, and they did, by a tenth of a point at most. That's tiny.
beats.on_screen: "even days 50.7%" and "real calendar 50.8%" side by side, held ≥2 s.
beats.source_line: "Our simulation and exact calculation on national births, 2000–2014."

beats.title: WHY SO SMALL
beats.narration_text: About ninety six percent of days sit within ten percent of average, so the real calendar is close enough to even that the model barely notices. The wrong assumption was forgiving. Keep that in mind, because the third change breaks the model somewhere else entirely.
beats.on_screen: a strip of the 365 day-shares, with the ±10% band shaded and "96% of days inside" printed.

beats.title: THE WINDOW
beats.narration_text: Third change: how many days there are to land on. Squeeze it. Not twenty three people from anywhere in the year, but twenty three people all born inside the same ninety days. Ninety five point four percent. Same group size, a quarter of the calendar, and the odds go from a coin flip to nearly certain.
beats.on_screen: the 365 grid dims to a 90-cell band; dots drop only inside it; the counter reaches 95.4% beside "full year 50.8%", held ≥2 s.

beats.title: THE SWEEP
beats.narration_text: Let me slide the window. A full year: fifty point eight. Half a year: seventy seven. Ninety days: ninety five. Sixty days: ninety nine. Born in the same month: better than ninety nine point nine percent. And with a window of seven days, twenty three people can't avoid sharing, there aren't enough days.
beats.on_screen: the band shrinks across the grid; a five-row table (365, 180, 90, 60, 30 days with percentages) held ≥2 s.

beats.title: HOW MANY IT TAKES
beats.narration_text: Flip it around and ask how many people you need for even odds. Across a whole year, twenty three. Ninety day window: twelve. Sixty days: ten. A thirty day window: seven. A fortnight: five. A week: four.
beats.on_screen: the shrinking band with the head-count column beside it, all six values printed.

beats.title: WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED
beats.narration_text: Here is what I almost missed. Does the uneven calendar still matter inside those windows? A tenth of a point at most, again. Seasons weren't the story. Of the three things, the head count moves the odds the way you'd expect. The evenness of the days barely moves them. And the number of days decides almost everything.
beats.on_screen: the three chapter cards return, each with its reading: PEOPLE "12% → 99%", EVENNESS "50.7% → 50.8%", DAYS "50.8% → 95.4%". Real vs even values for the 90-day window (95.44 vs 95.40) printed side by side.

beats.title: THE RULE
beats.narration_text: Look at those head-counts again. Twenty three for three hundred and sixty five days. Twelve for ninety. Seven for thirty. They follow a rule. Take the square root of the days. Multiply by one point two. Add a half, and round. A year gives twenty three. Ninety days gives twelve. Thirty days gives seven. A week gives four. It is right for every window in this film, and never more than one person off anywhere from two slots to two thousand.
beats.on_screen: the rule printed as one line, then a table of days, √days, rule result, exact answer for 365, 180, 90, 60, 30, 14, 7, held ≥3 s with the match column highlighted. Under it, the honest tally: "exact for 1,161 of 1,999 slot counts; off by one for the other 838; never more". The rule line carries "round halves up".
beats.source_line: "Our calculation. Checked against the exact answer for every slot count from 2 to 2,000."

beats.title: THE SCHOOL YEAR
beats.narration_text: A fair objection: classmates are all about the same age. But a school year with a cutoff date still contains every day of the calendar once, so it behaves like the full year, about fifty point eight percent. The squeeze only happens if the group is pinned to a narrow stretch of days.
beats.on_screen: the 365-day band labelled "one school-year cohort covers every day once".

beats.title: A NEW CASE
beats.narration_text: Now use it on something that isn't a birthday. Birth months: twelve slots. The square root of twelve is about three and a half. Times one point two, plus a half, rounds to five. So five people are enough for even odds that two share a birth month, if every month were equally likely. Four people give forty three percent. Five give sixty two.
beats.on_screen: twelve month-cells; the rule line worked step by step; 43% and 62% printed side by side.

beats.title: YOUR TURN
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Everyone in a class picks a random number from one to fifty. How many people before two probably match? Use the rule. A tempting wrong answer is half the slots, twenty five. Pause, work it out, and I'll say.
beats.on_screen: "50 slots. How many people for even odds?" with the rule line printed under it. After the narration, an **8 s hold** with a silent countdown bar.

beats.title: THE ANSWER
beats.narration_text: The root of fifty is about seven. Times one point two, plus a half, rounds to nine. Nine people give fifty three percent. Eight give forty five. Not twenty five. The slots set the scale, and their square root sets the crowd.
beats.on_screen: the working shown step by step; "9 people: 53%" beside "8 people: 45%"; the wrong answer "25 (half the slots)" struck through, held ≥2 s.

beats.title: OUTRO
beats.narration_text: Next time someone quotes odds that two things match, ask how many slots they could fall into. The square root of that number is about how many it takes. Tanmay Kulkarni, in for Humanitarians AI.
beats.on_screen: the rule line alone on screen; end card.
